title: Setting up a budget should [[give something back]] along the way.
hook: MuCoin is a personal-finance app concept, and this is its setup: five steps that take a person from their income to a first budget they have checked themselves.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Flow, screen design, prototype and written rationale

facts.label: For
facts.value: A design assignment set by a company

facts.label: Platform
facts.value: Setup flow for a personal-finance app, as a clickable Figma prototype

facts.label: Methods
facts.value: Double Diamond process, three usability rules (Hick, Miller, Jakob), a plan of 18 measures

linksHeading: The prototype and the written rationale
summary: The problem: a budgeting app has to ask what you earn and spend before it can help. Those numbers are private and hard to remember, and a long form gives nothing back until the end.
What I did: I designed a five-step setup (income, fixed expenses, variable expenses, saving goals, review), made it a clickable prototype and wrote down the reason for every screen.
The key idea: ask for a little, then show what it adds up to. Each expense step ends with a chart and a total, and the last step lets the person fix anything.
Where it stands: a concept. It has not been built or tested. I set targets for 18 measures, and none of them has been measured.

lead.alt: Five schematic screens in a row: income, fixed expenses, variable expenses, saving goals and review, each under a progress bar
lead.caption: The whole setup, left to right: income, fixed expenses, variable expenses, saving goals and review. These are schematics I drew from my rationale. The real screens are in the Figma prototype.

sections.label: The problem
sections.heading: A budgeting app asks its hardest questions first

blocks.p: A budgeting app can only help once it knows what you earn and what you spend. So the first thing it does is ask. Income is a private number. Expenses are hard to remember, and there are many of them.
If setup is one long form, the person does all of that work before they see anything useful. I wanted the setup itself to give something back along the way.

figures.alt: Diagram comparing one long setup form, which shows a result only at the end, with MuCoin's five steps that show results as they go
figures.caption: The idea in one picture. In the top row the first useful view comes after all the work. In MuCoin each expense step ends with a chart and a total. This is an illustration, not a measured comparison.

aside.title: What you are looking at.
aside.detail: MuCoin is a concept. It has not been built or tested with users. The real screens are in the Figma prototype linked on this page. The pictures here are diagrams I drew from my written rationale, so they show what each screen holds and why. They do not show its final look.

sections.label: My approach
sections.heading: I wrote down a reason for every screen

blocks.p: This was a solo project. I followed the Double Diamond, a design process with four stages: discover, define, develop and deliver. Here is what I have to show for each stage, including what has not happened yet.

figures.alt: Diagram of four stages, discover, define, develop and deliver, with what exists for each and two items marked as not done
figures.caption: Read the last card first. The flow was designed and prototyped, and the measures were planned. No test has been run.

blocks.p: For each screen I leaned on a well-known usability rule. These rules are short summaries of how people tend to behave. Each one gave me a reason to keep a screen small or familiar.

figures.alt: Three cards explaining Hick's Law, Miller's Law and Jakob's Law in plain words, each with where it is used in MuCoin
figures.caption: Each rule is at the top of its card in plain words. The green box says where it shows up in the flow.

blocks.p: I wrote all of this up as an 11-page rationale. One page covers the name and the process, four pages go through the flow screen by screen, and six pages define how each screen would be measured.

figures.alt: A page of the written rationale covering the expense summary and the variable expenses screen
figures.caption: A page from the flow section. It explains the expense summary and why the variable-expense screen copies the fixed-expense one.

figures.alt: A page of the written rationale listing measures for the goals screen, each with a definition, goal, measurement and target
figures.caption: A page from the measures section. Every measure has a definition, a goal, a way to count it and a target.

sections.label: The design
sections.heading: Income gets two fields and nothing more

blocks.p: Income is the first step, and it is a private number. I did not want the screen to scare anyone off. So it asks for two things only: the amount and where it comes from.

figures.alt: Schematic of the income step with five numbered notes: progress bar, amount with currency, source dropdown, add another source, and help and privacy links
figures.caption: The income step, part by part. Look at 5: the help and privacy links are on this step and stay on every step after it.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: Two fields cannot describe every kind of income. Someone who is paid irregularly, or who is unsure of the exact figure, still needs a way to answer honestly. A short form should not force a wrong number.

sections.label: The design
sections.heading: Expenses go in one at a time, then add up on screen

blocks.p: Fixed expenses stay the same each month. Variable expenses change. Listing all of them in detail is where I expected people to give up, because nobody holds a whole month of spending in their head.
So the step starts empty, with one prompt. Each expense goes through a short form: the details, a category and an optional comment.

figures.alt: Three schematic states of the expense step: an empty screen with a prompt, a short form, and a summary with a pie chart, a table and a total
figures.caption: Three states of the expense step, left to right. The form in the middle is the only thing a person has to learn.

blocks.p: Once an expense is entered, the person sees a summary. This is the part that gives something back: real numbers about their own money, before setup is finished.

figures.alt: Schematic of the expense summary with four numbered notes: pie chart, summary table, total in bold, and total as a share of income
figures.caption: The summary, part by part. Look at 4: the total is shown as a share of income, which ties this step back to the first one.

blocks.p: The variable-expense step uses the same three states. By then the pattern is familiar, so I expected it to go faster. That is a guess I have not tested.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: A chart is only as good as what was typed in. If someone is guessing, the summary should read as an estimate and not as a precise account.

blocks.p: This step was first called Financial goals. In informal research with a small group of users, Saving goals appealed more, so I renamed it. My write-up does not say how many people that was, so I treat it as a hint and not as a finding.

The step opens with a question: how much are you looking to save? Under it are suggested amounts, shown as shares of the person's income. After that they can set a goal of their own or pick a suggested one.

figures.alt: Flow diagram of the goals step: savings prompt, suggested amounts, set a goal, the goal form, and a celebration animation
figures.caption: The goals step in order. The celebration at the end is there so that setting one goal makes people want to set another.

figures.alt: Schematic of the goal form with five numbered notes: goal name, target amount, amount already saved, reminder, and icon
figures.caption: The goal form, part by part. It looks like the expense form on purpose, so it is already familiar.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: The icons and the celebration make this the longest step. I set its time target at 3 to 5 minutes, against 1 to 2 minutes for an expense step. Whether that extra time helps people or loses them is something only a test can show.

sections.label: The design
sections.heading: The last step is a check, and everything can still be changed

blocks.p: The final step shows everything the person entered, grouped into three sections: Income, Expenses and Goals. Each section opens and closes, and each entry can be edited. Editing goes back to a form the person already knows.

figures.alt: Schematic of the review step with five numbered notes: full progress bar, three sections, open and close, edit links, and confirm
figures.caption: The review, part by part. Look at 4: an edit returns to the same form the entry came from.

blocks.p: I wanted this step to do two jobs. It lets people catch mistakes while the numbers are fresh. It also gives setup a clear end, so the person feels finished and in control of what they shared.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: In my rationale I wrote that this screen would ensure a 100% completion rate. No screen can promise that. A review also adds one more screen before the person gets into the app, so it has to earn its place by catching real errors.

sections.label: Measures
sections.heading: Eighteen measures, each with a target

blocks.p: A KPI, or key performance indicator, is a number you track to see whether something is working. I defined 18 of them across the five steps. The two expense steps share the same four. For each one I wrote what it counts, how to count it and the number I would aim for.

figures.alt: Chart of fourteen percentage targets on a scale from 0 to 100 percent, grouped by income, expenses, saving goals and review
figures.caption: The fourteen targets that are percentages, on one scale. Dark bars are zones where higher is better. Pale bars are drop-off, where lower is better. These are aims, not results.

aside.title: Targets, not results.
aside.detail: None of these numbers has been measured. My rationale does not say where each target came from, so they are starting points for a test and nothing more. The Expenses rows apply to the fixed step and again to the variable step.

blocks.p: Reading the targets again, some of them do not hold up. I would fix these before running any test.

figures.alt: Three cards, each pairing something written in the rationale with what the author thinks of it now
figures.caption: Each card shows what I wrote in pink and what I think now in green. The middle card matters most: a corrected number is a good outcome, not a failure.

blocks.p: A smaller one sits beside these. I set a target for how often the celebration plays after a goal is set. It plays every time, so that number would only tell me whether the animation works. It says nothing about how people feel.
The measure I care about most now is corrections. Someone who notices a wrong amount and fixes it has a better budget than someone who finished fast with the wrong numbers.

Mu is the Greek letter μ. It is often used to mean micro, and in statistics it stands for the mean, or average. Both fit a budgeting app, where small amounts and averages matter. Despite the word coin, MuCoin has nothing to do with cryptocurrency.

figures.alt: The MuCoin logo, a gold coin stamped with the Greek letter mu beside the name, with three notes on what the name means
figures.caption: The logo and the three ideas behind the name. Look at the coin: it carries the letter μ.

blocks.p: For colour I wanted a mix of formal and casual. Money is a heavy subject, and the look was meant to make it feel a little lighter.

sections.label: What comes next
sections.heading: What I would do before building it

blocks.p: The flow is designed and the measures are written. The next job is to find out whether any of it is true.

steps.title: Test it with real people.
steps.detail: Watch each step: who finishes, how long it takes to reach a useful summary, and which errors get caught at review.

steps.title: Compare it with a shorter path.
steps.detail: Try a short version with optional detail against this five-step sequence, and see which one people complete.

steps.title: Include the awkward cases.
steps.detail: Irregular income, rough estimates and skipped answers, as well as tidy inputs.

steps.title: Ask about privacy.
steps.detail: Check that people understand what happens to the numbers they enter.

sections.label: What I learned
sections.heading: A target is a guess until it is tested

blocks.p: The flow rests on one idea I still believe in: give people something back while they are still entering their numbers. A summary after each step is a reason to keep going and a chance to fix a mistake.
What I would change is how I wrote about it. I stated some targets as if they were outcomes. Next time I would write each one as a question, run a small test, and only then put numbers on the page.
